listen_text: Section. Introduction. One question that interests modal logicians is the relationship between the accessibility relation and the truth of certain formulas in models with that accessibility relation. For instance, suppose the accessibility relation is reflexive, that is, for every w belongs to W , R relates w to itself . In other words, every world is accessible from itself. That means that when necessarily A is true at a world w , w itself is among the accessible worlds at which A must therefore be true. So, if the accessibility relation R of M is reflexive, then whatever world w and formula A we take, if necessarily A, then A will be true there (in other words, the schema if necessarily p, then p and all its substitution instances are true in M ). The converse, however, is false. It's not the case, for example, that if if necessarily p, then p is true in M , then R is reflexive. For we can easily find a non-reflexive model M where if necessarily p, then p is true at all worlds: take the model with a single world w , not accessible from itself, but with w belongs to V of p . By picking the truth value of p suitably, we can make if necessarily A, then A true in a model that is not reflexive. The solution is to remove the variable assignment V from the equation. If we require that if necessarily p, then p is true at all worlds in M , regardless of which worlds are in V of p , then it is necessary that R is reflexive. For in any non-reflexive model, there will be at least one world w such that not R relates w to itself . If we set V of p equals W with w removed , then p will be true at all worlds other than w , and so at all worlds accessible from w (since w is guaranteed not to be accessible from w , and w is the only world where p is false). On the other hand, p is false at w , so if necessarily p, then p is false at w . This suggests that we should introduce a notation for model structures without a valuation: we call these frames. A frame F is simply a pair the ordered pair W, R consisting of a set of worlds with an accessibility relation. Every model the ordered triple W, R, V is then, as we say, based on the frame the ordered pair W, R . Conversely, a frame determines the class of models based on it; and a class of frames determines the class of models which are based on any frame in the class. And we can define A is valid in frame F , the notion of a formula being valid in a frame as: A is true in modal model M for all M based on F . With this notation, we can establish correspondence relations between formulas and classes of frames: for example, the conditional from necessarily p to p is valid in frame F if, and only if, F is reflexive. End section.

listen_text: Section. Properties of Accessibility Relations. Many modal formulas turn out to be characteristic of simple, and even familiar, properties of the accessibility relation. In one direction, that means that any model that has a given property makes a corresponding formula (and all its substitution instances) true. We begin with five classical examples of kinds of accessibility relations and the formulas the truth of which they guarantee. Theorem. Let modal model M equals the ordered triple W, R, V be a model. If R has the property on the left side of the table of five classical correspondence facts , every instance of the formula on the right side is true in M . End theorem. Table. t. Five classical correspondence facts. Header: if R has the named property, then the paired formula is true in M . Serial row. Relation condition: for every u there exists a v such that R relates u to v . Modal schema: if necessarily p, then possibly p , labelled axiom D . Reflexive row. Relation condition: for every w, R relates w to itself . Modal schema: if necessarily p, then p , labelled axiom T . Symmetric row. The source first prints the modal schema if p, then necessarily possibly p , labelled axiom B , then on the following line its relation condition for every u and v, if R relates u to v, then R relates v to u . Transitive row. The source first prints the modal schema if necessarily p, then necessarily necessarily p , labelled axiom four , then its relation condition for every u, v, and w, if R relates u to v and R relates v to w, then R relates u to w . Euclidean row. The source first prints the modal schema if possibly p, then necessarily possibly p , labelled axiom five , then its relation condition for every w, u, and v, if R relates w to u and R relates w to v, then R relates u to v . End table. Caption. Five correspondence facts. End caption. End table. Proof. Here is the case for axiom B: to show that the schema is true in a model we need to show that all of its instances are true at all worlds in the model. So let if A, then necessarily possibly A be a given instance of axiom B, and let w belongs to W be an arbitrary world. Suppose the antecedent A is true at w , in order to show that necessarily possibly A is true at w . So we need to show that possibly A is true at all w prime accessible from w . Now, for any w prime such that R relates w to w prime we have, using the hypothesis of symmetry, that also R relates w prime to w (see the two-world figure illustrating the symmetry argument ). Since A is true in modal model M at world w , we have possibly A is true in modal model M at world w prime . Since w prime was an arbitrary world such that R relates w to w prime , we have necessarily possibly A is true in modal model M at world w . We leave the other cases as exercises. End proof. Exercise. Complete the proof of the theorem that five accessibility properties guarantee their corresponding modal schemas . End exercise. This exercise remains unsolved. Figure. Two-world accessibility graph for symmetry. The first node annotations, in source order, are A is true at this world and necessarily possibly A is true at this world . That node is world w . The second node annotation is possibly A is true at this world . That node is world w prime . The first directed arrow goes from w to w prime. The second directed arrow goes from w prime back to w. No loops, additional worlds, additional valuations, or other accessibility arrows are printed. End diagram. Caption. The argument from symmetry. End caption. End figure. Notice that the converse implications of the theorem that five accessibility properties guarantee their corresponding modal schemas do not hold: it's not true that if a model verifies a schema, then the accessibility relation of that model has the corresponding property. In the case of axiom T and reflexive models, it is easy to give an example of a model in which axiom T itself fails: let W is the singleton set containing w and V of p equals the empty set . Then R is not reflexive, but necessarily p is true in modal model M at world w and p is false in modal model M at world w . But here we have just a single instance of axiom T that fails in M ; other instances, for example, if necessarily not p, then not p are true. It is harder to give examples where every substitution instance of axiom T is true in M and M is not reflexive. But there are such models, too: Proposition. Let modal model M equals the ordered triple W, R, V be a model such that W equals the set containing u and v , where worlds u and v are related by R : that is, both R relates u to v and R relates v to u . Suppose that for all p : u belongs to V of p if and only if v belongs to V of p . Then: List. Next item. For all A : A is true in modal model M at world u if and only if A is true in modal model M at world v (use induction on A ). Next item. Every instance of axiom T is true in M . End list. Since M is not reflexive (it is, in fact, irreflexive ), the converse of the theorem that five accessibility properties guarantee their corresponding modal schemas fails in the case of axiom T (similar arguments can be given for some—though not all—the other schemas mentioned in the theorem that five accessibility properties guarantee their corresponding modal schemas ). End proposition. Source anomaly note. Source hypothesis caveat. The proposition states that R contains the two cross-world arrows R u v and R v u, but it does not state that the self-loops R u u and R v v are absent. Its concluding assertion that the model is non-reflexive, indeed irreflexive, therefore needs the additional intended condition that those self-loops are absent. The printed proposition and its unsolved exercise are retained unchanged. Original source remains available in Source view. End note. Exercise. Prove the claims in the proposition about the two-world model in which every T instance is true . End exercise. This exercise remains unsolved. Although we will focus on the five classical formulas axiom D, axiom T, axiom B, axiom four, and axiom five, we record in the table of five additional correspondence facts a few more properties of accessibility relations. The accessibility relation R is partially functional, if from every world at most one world is accessible. If it is the case that from every world exactly one world is accessible, we call it functional. (Thus the functional relations are precisely those that are both serial and partially functional). They are called “functional” because the accessibility relation operates like a (partial) function. A relation is weakly dense if whenever R relates u to v , there is a w “between” u and v . So weakly dense relations are in a sense the opposite of transitive relations: in a transitive relation, whenever you can reach v from u by a detour via w , you can reach v from u directly; in a weakly dense relation, whenever you can reach v from u directly, you can also reach it by a detour via some w . A relation is weakly directed if whenever you can reach worlds u and v from some world w , you can reach a single world t from both u and v —this is sometimes called the “diamond property” or “confluence.” Table. t. Five additional correspondence facts. Header: if R has the named property, then the paired formula is true in M . Partially functional row. Modal schema: if possibly p, then necessarily p . Relation condition: for every w, u, and v, if R relates w to u and R relates w to v, then u equals v . Functional row. Relation condition: for every w there exists a v such that, for every u, R relates w to u if and only if u equals v . Modal schema: possibly p if and only if necessarily p . Weakly dense row. Modal schema: if necessarily necessarily p, then necessarily p . Relation condition: for every u and v, if R relates u to v, then there exists a w such that R relates u to w and R relates w to v . Weakly connected row. Modal schema: either it is necessary that, if p and necessarily p, then q; or it is necessary that, if q and necessarily q, then p , labelled axiom L . Relation condition: For every w, u, and v, if R relates w to u and R relates w to v, then either R relates u to v, u equals v, or R relates v to u. . Weakly directed row. Modal schema: if possibly necessarily p, then necessarily possibly p , labelled axiom G . Relation condition: For every w, u, and v, if R relates w to u and R relates w to v, then there exists t such that R relates u to t and R relates v to t. . End table. Caption. Five more correspondence facts. End caption. End table. Exercise. Let modal model M equals the ordered triple W, R, V be a model. Show that if R satisfies the left-hand properties of the table of five additional correspondence facts , every instance of the corresponding right-hand formula is true in M . End exercise. This exercise remains unsolved. End section.

listen_text: Section. Frames. Definition. A frame is a pair frame F equals the ordered pair W, R where W is a non-empty set of worlds and R a binary relation on W . A model M is based on a frame frame F equals the ordered pair W, R if and only if modal model M equals the ordered triple W, R, V for some valuation V . End definition. Definition. If F is a frame, we say that A is valid in F , A is valid in frame F , if A is true in modal model M for every model M based on F . If F is a class of frames, we say A is valid in F , A is valid in the class of frames F , if and only if A is valid in frame F for every frame frame F belongs to the class of frames F . End definition. The reason frames are interesting is that correspondence between schemas and properties of the accessibility relation R is at the level of frames, not of models. For instance, although axiom T is true in all reflexive models, not every model in which axiom T is true is reflexive. However, it is true that not only is axiom T valid on all reflexive frames, also every frame in which axiom T is valid is reflexive. Remark. Validity in a class of frames is a special case of the notion of validity in a class of models: A is valid in the class of frames F if and only if A is valid in the class of models C where C is the class of all models based on a frame in F . Obviously, if a formula or a schema is valid, that is, valid with respect to the class of all models, it is also valid with respect to any class F of frames. End remark. Disclosed reader correction. The source remark is announced as a remark and its closing boundary is preserved. Its prose and mathematics are unchanged. Original source remains available in Source view. End note. End section.

listen_text: Section. Frame Definability. Even though the converse implications of the theorem that five accessibility properties guarantee their corresponding modal schemas fail, they hold if we replace “model” by “frame”: for the properties considered in the theorem that five accessibility properties guarantee their corresponding modal schemas , it is true that if a formula is valid in a frame then the accessibility relation of that frame has the corresponding property. So, the formulas considered define the classes of frames that have the corresponding property. Definition. If F is a class of frames, we say A defines F if and only if A is valid in frame F for all and only frames frame F belongs to the class of frames F . End definition. We now proceed to establish the full definability results for frames. Theorem. If the formula on the right side of the table of five classical correspondence facts is valid in a frame F , then F has the property on the left side. End theorem. Proof. List. Next item. Suppose axiom D is valid in frame F equals the ordered pair W, R , that is, the conditional from necessarily p to possibly p is valid in frame F . Let modal model M equals the ordered triple W, R, V be a model based on F , and w belongs to W . We have to show that there is a v such that R relates w to v . Suppose not: then both necessarily A is true in modal model M and possibly A is false in modal model M at world w for any A , including p . But then the conditional from necessarily p to possibly p is false in modal model M at world w , contradicting the assumption that the conditional from necessarily p to possibly p is valid in frame F . Next item. Suppose axiom T is valid in F , that is, the conditional from necessarily p to p is valid in frame F . Let w belongs to W be an arbitrary world; we need to show R relates w to itself . Let u belongs to V of p if and only if R relates w to u (when q is other than p , V of q is arbitrary, say V of q equals the empty set, followed by a closing parenthesis . Let modal model M equals the ordered triple W, R, V . By construction, for all u such that R relates w to u : p is true in modal model M at world u , and hence necessarily p is true in modal model M at world w . But by hypothesis if necessarily p, then p is true at w , so that p is true in modal model M at world w , but by definition of V this is possible only if R relates w to itself . Next item. We prove the contrapositive: Suppose F is not symmetric, we show that axiom B, that is, if p, then necessarily possibly p is not valid in frame F equals the ordered pair W, R . If F is not symmetric, there are u , v belongs to W such that R relates u to v but not R relates v to u . Define V such that w belongs to V of p if and only if not R relates v to w (and V is arbitrary otherwise). Let modal model M equals the ordered triple W, R, V . Now, by definition of V , p is true in modal model M at world w for all w such that not R relates v to w , in particular, p is true in modal model M at world u since not R relates v to u . Also, since R relates v to w if and only if w does not belong to V of p , there is no w such that R relates v to w and p is true in modal model M at world w , and hence possibly p is false in modal model M at world v . Since R relates u to v , also necessarily possibly p is false in modal model M at world u . It follows that the conditional from p to necessarily possibly p is false in modal model M at world u , and so axiom B is not valid in F . Next item. Suppose axiom four is valid in frame F equals the ordered pair W, R , that is, the conditional from necessarily p to necessarily necessarily p is valid in frame F , and let u , v , w belongs to W be arbitrary worlds such that R relates u to v and R relates v to w ; we need to show that R relates u to w . Define V such that z belongs to V of p if and only if R relates u to z (and V is arbitrary otherwise). Let modal model M equals the ordered triple W, R, V . By definition of V , p is true in modal model M at world z for all z such that R relates u to z , and hence necessarily p is true in modal model M at world u . But by hypothesis axiom four, if necessarily p, then necessarily necessarily p , is true at u , so that necessarily necessarily p is true in modal model M at world u . Since R relates u to v and R relates v to w , we have p is true in modal model M at world w , but by definition of V this is possible only if R relates u to w , as desired. Next item. We proceed contrapositively, assuming that the frame frame F equals the ordered pair W, R is not euclidean, and show that it falsifies axiom five, that is, the conditional from possibly p to necessarily possibly p is not valid in frame F . Suppose there are worlds u , v , w belongs to W such that R relates w to u and R relates w to v but not R relates u to v . Define V such that for all worlds z , z belongs to V of p if and only if it is not the case that R relates u to z . Let modal model M equals the ordered triple W, R, V . Then by hypothesis p is true in modal model M at world v and since R relates w to v also possibly p is true in modal model M at world w . However, there is no world y such that R relates u to y and p is true in modal model M at world y so possibly p is false in modal model M at world u . Since R relates w to u , it follows that necessarily possibly p is false in modal model M at world w , so that axiom five, if possibly p, then necessarily possibly p , fails at w . End list. End proof. Source anomaly note. Source notation caveat. This sentence is evaluating both modal formulas at the chosen world w. The diamond assertion prints the world argument w, while the immediately paired box assertion omits it. The omission is retained and identified; this edition does not insert a hidden world argument into the source formula. Original source remains available in Source view. End note. You'll notice a difference between the proof for axiom D and the other cases: no mention was made of the valuation V . In effect, we proved that if axiom D is true in modal model M then M is serial. So axiom D defines the class of serial models, not just frames. Corollary. Any model where axiom D is true is serial. End corollary. Corollary. Each formula on the right side of the table of five classical correspondence facts defines the class of frames which have the property on the left side. End corollary. Proof. In the theorem that five accessibility properties guarantee their corresponding modal schemas , we proved that if a model has the property on the left, the formula on the right is true in it. Thus, if a frame F has the property on the left, the formula on the right is valid in F . In the full correspondence theorem for D, T, B, four, and five , we proved the converse implications: if a formula on the right is valid in F , F has the property on the left. End proof. Exercise. Show that if the formula on the right side of the table of five additional correspondence facts is valid in a frame F , then F has the property on the left side. To do this, consider a frame that does not satisfy the property on the left, and define a suitable V such that the formula on the right is false at some world. End exercise. This exercise remains unsolved. the full correspondence theorem for D, T, B, four, and five also shows that the properties can be combined: for instance if both axiom B and axiom four are valid in F then the frame is both symmetric and transitive, etc. Many important modal logics are characterized as the set of formulas valid in all frames that combine some frame properties, and so we can characterize them as the set of formulas valid in all frames in which the corresponding defining formulas are valid. For instance, the classical system Sfour is the set of all formulas valid in all reflexive and transitive frames, that is, in all those where both axiom T and axiom four are valid. Sfive is the set of all formulas valid in all reflexive, symmetric, and euclidean frames, that is, all those where all of axiom T, axiom B, and axiom five are valid. Logical relationships between properties of R in general correspond to relationships between the corresponding defining formulas. For instance, every reflexive relation is serial; hence, whenever axiom T is valid in a frame, so is axiom D. (Note that this relationship is not that of entailment. It is not the case that whenever axiom T is true in modal model M at world w then axiom D is true in modal model M at world w .) We record some such relationships. Proposition. Let R be a binary relation on a set W ; then: List. Next item. If R is reflexive, then it is serial. Next item. If R is symmetric, then it is transitive if and only if it is euclidean. Next item. If R is symmetric or euclidean then it is weakly directed (it has the “diamond property”). Next item. If R is euclidean then it is weakly connected. Next item. If R is functional then it is serial. End list. End proposition. Exercise. Prove the proposition on five implications among accessibility properties . End exercise. This exercise remains unsolved. End section.

listen_text: Section. First-order Definability. We've seen that a number of properties of accessibility relations of frames can be defined by modal formulas. For instance, symmetry of frames can be defined by the formula axiom B, if p, then necessarily possibly p . The conditions we've encountered so far can all be expressed by first-order formulas in a language involving a single two-place predicate symbol. For instance, symmetry is defined by for every x and every y, if Q relates x to y, then Q relates y to x in the sense that a first-order structure M with the domain of structure M equals W and the interpretation of Q in structure M equals R satisfies the preceding formula if and only if R is symmetric. This suggests the following definition: Definition. A class F of frames is first-order definable if there is a sentence A in the first-order language with a single two-place predicate symbol Q such that frame F, equal to the ordered pair W, R, belongs to the class of frames F if and only if structure M satisfies A in the first-order structure M with the domain of structure M equals W and the interpretation of Q in structure M equals R . End definition. It turns out that the properties and modal formulas that define them considered so far are exceptional. Not every formula defines a first-order definable class of frames, and not every first-order definable class of frames is definable by a modal formula. A counterexample to the first is given by the Loeb formula: Displayed expression. axiom W, the Loeb formula: if it is necessary that necessarily p implies p, then necessarily p. End displayed expression. axiom W defines the class of transitive and converse well-founded frames. A relation is well-founded if there is no infinite sequence w subscript one , w subscript two , and so on such that R relates w subscript two to w subscript one , R relates w subscript three to w subscript two , and so on. For instance, the relation the less than relation on the natural numbers is well-founded, whereas the relation the less than relation on the integers is not. A relation is converse well-founded if and only if its converse is well-founded. So converse well-founded relations are those where there is no infinite sequence w subscript one , w subscript two , and so on such that R relates w subscript one to w subscript two , R relates w subscript two to w subscript three , and so on. There is, however, no first-order formula defining transitive converse well-founded relations. For suppose structure M satisfies F if and only if R equals the interpretation of Q in structure M is transitive converse well-founded. Let A subscript n be the formula Displayed expression. the conjunction of Q relating a subscript one to a subscript two, continuing through Q relating a subscript n minus one to a subscript n. End displayed expression. Now consider the set of formulas Displayed expression. Gamma equals the set containing F and A subscript one, A subscript two, and so on. End displayed expression. Every finite subset of Gamma is satisfiable: Let k be largest such that A subscript k is in the subset, the domain of structure M subscript k equals the set of integers from one through k , the interpretation of a subscript i in structure M subscript k equals i , and the interpretation of Q in structure M subscript k equals the less than relation . Since the less than relation on the set of integers from one through k is transitive and converse well-founded, structure M subscript k satisfies F . structure M subscript k satisfies A subscript i by construction, for all i is less than or equal to k . By the Compactness Theorem for first-order logic, Gamma is satisfiable in some structure M . By hypothesis, since structure M satisfies F , the relation the interpretation of Q in structure M is converse well-founded. But clearly, the interpretation of a subscript one in structure M , the interpretation of a subscript two in structure M , and so on would form an infinite sequence of the kind ruled out by converse well-foundedness. A counterexample to the second claim is given by the property of universality: for every u and v , R relates u to v . Universal frames are first-order definable by the formula for every x and every y, Q relates x to y . However, no modal formula is valid in all and only the universal frames. This is a consequence of a result that is independently interesting: the formulas valid in universal frames are exactly the same as those valid in reflexive, symmetric, and transitive frames. There are reflexive, symmetric, and transitive frames that are not universal, hence every formula valid in all universal frames is also valid in some non-universal frames. End section.

listen_text: Section. Equivalence Relations and Sfive. The modal logic Sfive is characterized as the set of formulas valid on all universal frames, that is, every world is accessible from every world, including itself. In such a scenario, the necessity operator corresponds to necessity and the possibility operator to possibility: necessarily A is true if A is true at every world, and possibly A is true if A is true at some world. It turns out that Sfive can also be characterized as the formulas valid on all reflexive, symmetric, and transitive frames, that is, on all equivalence relations. Definition. A binary relation R on W is an equivalence relation if and only if it is reflexive, symmetric and transitive. A relation R on W is universal if and only if R relates u to v for all u and v belong to W . End definition. Since axiom T, axiom B, and axiom four characterize the reflexive, symmetric, and transitive frames, the frames where the accessibility relation is an equivalence relation are exactly those in which all three formulas are valid. It turns out that the equivalence relations can also be characterized by other combinations of formulas, since the conditions with which we've defined equivalence relations are equivalent to combinations of other familiar conditions on R . Proposition. The following are equivalent: List. Next item. R is an equivalence relation; Next item. R is reflexive and euclidean; Next item. R is serial, symmetric, and euclidean; Next item. R is serial, symmetric, and transitive. End list. End proposition. Proof. Exercise. End proof. Exercise. Prove the proposition giving four equivalent characterizations of equivalence relations by showing: List. Next item. If R is symmetric and transitive, it is euclidean. Next item. If R is reflexive, it is serial. Next item. If R is reflexive and euclidean, it is symmetric. Next item. If R is symmetric and euclidean, it is transitive. Next item. If R is serial, symmetric, and transitive, it is reflexive. End list. Explain why this suffices for the proof that the conditions are equivalent. End exercise. This exercise remains unsolved. the proposition giving four equivalent characterizations of equivalence relations is the semantic counterpart to the later proposition listing four equivalent axiomatizations of S five , in that it gives an equivalent characterization of the modal logic of frames over which R is an equivalence relation (the logic traditionally referred to as Sfive). What is the relationship between universal and equivalence relations? Although every universal relation is an equivalence relation, clearly not every equivalence relation is universal. However, the formulas valid on all universal relations are exactly the same as those valid on all equivalence relations. Proposition. Let R be an equivalence relation, and for each w belongs to W define the equivalence class of w as the set the equivalence class of w equals the set of worlds w prime in W such that R relates w to w prime . Then: List. Next item. w belongs to its equivalence class ; Next item. R is universal on each equivalence class open bracket w close bracket ; Next item. The collection of equivalence classes partitions W into mutually exclusive and jointly exhaustive subsets. End list. End proposition. Proposition. A formula A is valid in all frames frame F equals the ordered pair W, R where R is an equivalence relation, if and only if it is valid in all frames frame F equals the ordered pair W, R where R is universal. Hence, the logic of universal frames is just Sfive. End proposition. Proof. It's immediate to verify that a universal relation R on W is an equivalence. Hence, if A is valid in all frames where R is an equivalence it is valid in all universal frames. For the other direction, we argue contrapositively: suppose B is a formula that fails at a world w in a model modal model M equals the ordered triple W, R, V based on a frame the ordered pair W, R , where R is an equivalence on W . So B is false in modal model M at world w . Define a model modal model M prime equals the ordered triple W prime, R prime, V prime as follows: List. Next item. W prime equals the equivalence class of w ; Next item. R prime is universal on W prime ; Next item. V prime of p equals the intersection of V of p with W prime . End list. (So the set W prime of worlds in M prime is represented by the shaded area in the figure partitioning W into equivalence classes .) It is easy to see that R and R prime agree on W prime . Then one can show by induction on formulas that for all w prime belongs to W prime : A is true in modal model M prime at world w prime if and only if A is true in modal model M at world w prime for each A (this makes sense since W prime is a subset of W ). In particular, B is false in modal model M prime at world w , and B fails in a model based on a universal frame. End proof. Figure. t. Equivalence-class partition diagram. An outer rounded rectangle represents W. Two curved boundaries divide it into the four labelled regions. The gray shaded region represents W prime, equal to the equivalence class of w, as stated immediately before the figure. This is a partition picture, not a Kripke accessibility graph: it prints no directed edges, relation labels, worlds inside the classes, or valuations. End diagram. Caption. listen_text: Section. Second-order Definability. Not every frame property definable by modal formulas is first-order definable. However, if we allow quantification over one-place predicates (that is, monadic second-order quantification), we define all modally definable frame properties. The trick is to exploit a systematic way in which the conditions under which a modal formula is true at a world are related to first-order formulas. This is the so-called standard translation of modal formulas into first-order formulas in a language containing not just a two-place predicate symbol Q for the accessibility relation, but also a one-place predicate symbol P subscript i for the propositional variables p subscript i occurring in A . Definition. The standard translation the standard translation at x of A is inductively defined as follows: List. Next item. Case: A is the falsity constant. the standard translation at x of the current formula equals falsity . Next item. Case: A is the propositional variable p subscript i. the standard translation at x of the current formula equals P subscript i of x . Next item. Case: A is the negation of B. the standard translation at x of the current formula equals the negation of the standard translation at x of B . Next item. Case: A is the conjunction of B and C. the standard translation at x of the current formula equals the conjunction of the standard translation at x of B and the standard translation at x of C . Next item. Case: A is the disjunction of B and C. the standard translation at x of the current formula equals the disjunction of the standard translation at x of B and the standard translation at x of C . Next item. Case: A is the conditional from B to C. the standard translation at x of the current formula equals the conditional from the standard translation at x of B to the standard translation at x of C . Next item. Case: A is necessarily B. the standard translation at x of the current formula equals: for every y, if Q relates x to y, then the standard translation at y of B . Next item. Case: A is possibly B. the standard translation at x of the current formula equals: there exists a y such that Q relates x to y and the standard translation at y of B . End list. End definition. For instance, the standard translation at x of the conditional from necessarily p to p is if, for every y, Q relates x to y only if P holds of y, then P holds of x . Any structure for the language of the standard translation at x of A requires a domain, a two-place relation assigned to Q , and subsets of the domain assigned to the one-place predicate symbols P subscript i . In other words, the components of such a structure are exactly those of a model for A : the domain is the set of worlds, the two-place relation assigned to Q is the accessibility relation, and the subsets assigned to P subscript i are just the assignments V of p subscript i . It won't surprise that satisfaction of A in a modal model and of the standard translation at x of A in the corresponding structure agree: Proposition. Let modal model M equals the ordered triple W, R, V , M prime be the first-order structure with the domain of structure M prime equals W , the interpretation of Q in structure M prime equals R , and the interpretation of P subscript i in structure M prime equals V of p subscript i , and s of x equals w . Then Displayed expression. A is true in modal model M at world w if and only if structure M prime satisfies the standard translation at x of A under assignment s. End displayed expression. End proposition. Proof. By induction on A . End proof. Proposition. Suppose A is a modal formula and frame F equals the ordered pair W, R is a frame. Let F prime be the first-order structure with the domain of structure F prime equals W and the interpretation of Q in structure F prime equals R , and let A prime be the second-order formula Displayed expression. for every X subscript one through X subscript n, and every x, the result of simultaneously substituting X subscript one through X subscript n for P subscript one through P subscript n in the standard translation at x of A. End displayed expression. where P subscript one , and so on, P subscript n are all one-place predicate symbols in the standard translation at x of A . Then Displayed expression. A is valid in frame F if and only if structure F prime satisfies A prime. End displayed expression. End proposition. Proof. structure F prime satisfies A prime if and only if for every structure M prime where the interpretation of P subscript i in structure M prime is a subset of W for i equals one , and so on, n , and for every s with s of x belongs to W , structure M prime satisfies the standard translation at x of A under assignment s . By the proposition that the standard translation preserves truth at a world , that is the case if and only if for all models M based on F and every world w belongs to W , A is true in modal model M at world w , that is, A is valid in frame F . End proof. Definition. A class F of frames is second-order definable if there is a sentence A in the second-order language with a single two-place predicate symbol P and quantifiers only over monadic set variables such that frame F, equal to the ordered pair W, R, belongs to the class of frames F if and only if structure M satisfies A in the structure M with the domain of structure M equals W and the interpretation of P in structure M equals R . End definition. Corollary. If a class of frames is definable by a formula A , the corresponding class of accessibility relations is definable by a monadic second-order sentence. End corollary. Proof. The monadic second-order sentence A prime of the preceding proof has the required property. End proof. As an example, consider again the formula if necessarily p, then p . It defines reflexivity. Reflexivity is of course first-order definable by the sentence for every x, Q relates x to itself . But it is also definable by the monadic second-order sentence Displayed expression. for every set X and every x, if for every y, Q relates x to y only if X holds of y, then X holds of x. End displayed expression. This means, of course, that the two sentences are equivalent. Here's how you might convince yourself of this directly: First suppose the second-order sentence is true in a structure M . Since x and X are universally quantified, the remainder must hold for any x belongs to W and set X is a subset of W , for example, the set the set of z such that R relates x to z where R equals the interpretation of Q in structure M . So, for any s with s of x belongs to W and s of X equals the set of z such that R relates x to z we have structure M satisfies: if, for every y, Q relates x to y only if X holds of y, then X holds of x . But by the way we've picked s of X that means structure M satisfies: if for every y, Q relating x to y implies itself, then Q relates x to itself, under assignment s , which is equivalent to Q relates x to itself since the antecedent is valid. Since s of x is arbitrary, we have structure M satisfies that for every x, Q relates x to itself . Source anomaly note. Source notation caveat. The omission is preserved rather than silently supplied. Original source remains available in Source view. End note. Now suppose that structure M satisfies that for every x, Q relates x to itself and show that structure M satisfies: for every set X, for every x, if for every y, Q relates x to y only if X holds of y, then X holds of x . Pick any assignment s , and assume structure M satisfies that, for every y, if Q relates x to y then X holds of y, under assignment s . Let s prime be the y -variant of s with s prime of y equals s of x ; we have structure M satisfies the conditional from Q relating x to y to X holding of y, under assignment s prime , that is, structure M satisfies the conditional from Q relating x to itself to X holding of x, under assignment s . Since structure M satisfies that for every x, Q relates x to itself , the antecedent is true, and we have structure M satisfies X of x under assignment s , which is what we needed to show. Since some definable classes of frames are not first-order definable, not every monadic second-order sentence of the form A prime is equivalent to a first-order sentence. There is no effective method to decide which ones are. End section. End chapter.
